hero.title: Portfolio
hero.subtitle: Intentionally overengineered.
hero.introMarkdown: This portfolio is intentionally overengineered: a working demonstration of Aspire and a modular monolith. Clear ownership, repeatable startup and visible request flow are the point.

nodes.title: A small portfolio
nodes.markdown: Real page reads and contact submissions.

nodes.title: Aspire
nodes.markdown: Wire, run and observe the local stack.

blocks.captionMarkdown: Aspire handles the running pieces. Module boundaries handle the code inside the API. Neither requires turning the modules into microservices.

overview.title: Purpose
overview.markdown: An architecture demo with real workloads.

overview.title: Modular monolith
overview.markdown: Explicit ownership without separate service deployments.

sections.title: What the extra structure buys
sections.introMarkdown: Profiles, case studies and contact mail keep the examples small.

cards.title: One place to wire the stack
cards.markdown: AppHost centralizes endpoints, configuration and startup dependencies. One command starts the preview.

cards.title: Ownership you can check
cards.markdown: Three modules share an API, with implementation references checked by architecture tests.

cards.title: A visible side effect
cards.markdown: Local contact tests land in smtp4dev. Production sends real mail through Google Workspace, with credentials kept on the server.

sections.title: Three modules. One API.
sections.introMarkdown: One API process avoids a separate deployment and network boundary for each feature.

nodes.title: API host
nodes.markdown: Composes the modules; rules stay inside them.

rows: DTOs and contracts another module may reference.

EF Core storage or SMTP adapters.

blocks.markdown: Profile and Projects share a SQLite file, not tables or contexts. Contact stores no messages. Architecture tests reject foreign implementation references and cycles.

blocks.title: Where it's overengineered
blocks.markdown: A smaller app could serve this content. Extra projects and orchestration make the benefits inspectable; they aren't requirements for a portfolio. Aspire isn't a prerequisite for a modular monolith, either.

sections.title: Aspire: run it, then inspect it
sections.introMarkdown: In development, AppHost supplies API addresses and SMTP settings, then waits for dependencies. That replaces separate launch commands and manually synchronized configuration.

nodes.markdown: Service wiring, startup order and diagnostics.

nodes.title: API
nodes.markdown: Module endpoints; waits for mail capture.

nodes.title: smtp4dev
nodes.markdown: Capture mail without a live email account.

blocks.captionMarkdown: The local dashboard groups logs, HTTP traces and health by resource. SQLite uses a file; smtp4dev holds test mail. Production uses Docker and real SMTP, not the development stack.

cards.title: Follow a page read
cards.markdown: Open a case study and follow its frontend-to-API request in the dashboard. Projects owns the document.

cards.title: Inspect a side effect
cards.markdown: Submit the contact form and inspect its message in smtp4dev. The UI confirms local capture, not inbox delivery.

sections.title: The frontend, in brief
sections.introMarkdown: The frontend demonstrates prerendered WASM, not a persistent server circuit.

steps.title: Prerender
steps.markdown: The site host reads the API and returns populated HTML.

steps.title: Hand off
steps.markdown: Public data and error state travel with the page. WASM starts without fetching them again.

steps.title: Interact
steps.markdown: Palette, expanders and loaded examples run in the browser. New documents and email still need the API.

blocks.captionMarkdown: Browser requests use `/api` on the site origin; YARP forwards them to the backend. No Server or Auto render mode.

sections.title: Change, check, ship
sections.introMarkdown: Business changes stay in their module; UI stays in the frontend. GitHub Actions checks pull requests and main pushes; successful current-main builds deploy automatically.

blocks.markdown: Case studies are JSON documents with Markdown and typed blocks. Validation runs before import; stable IDs update records, while unlisted content is preserved.

blocks.title: Content changes
blocks.code:
bash scripts/dev.sh validate
bash scripts/dev.sh import
blocks.captionMarkdown: Content updates are explicit, never startup seeds.

blocks.title: Preview and checks
blocks.code:
bash scripts/dev.sh

# In another terminal:
PORTFOLIO_BROWSER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:5420 \
  bash scripts/verify.sh
blocks.captionMarkdown: Requires the pinned SDK and rootless Podman. Verify runs architecture/module/API tests, EF model checks and browser smoke. Use the same suite to check trimmed Release output.

steps.title: Verify
steps.markdown: Build and test the solution, validate content and check EF models against migrations. Browser smoke runs the published containers with fresh SQLite and disposable SMTP capture—not the live mailbox.

steps.title: Publish
steps.markdown: Reuse the tested publish outputs for three commit-tagged Docker images: frontend host, API and migration/import tool. Push them to GitHub Container Registry without rebuilding the application.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.markdown: A restricted SSH command serializes releases, snapshots SQLite, applies migrations and imports content. It starts the new containers, verifies populated HTTPS content and restores previous images/data if checks fail.

blocks.captionMarkdown: Nginx handles HTTPS. The non-root containers run the frontend and API; persistent data and secrets stay outside their images. Deployments briefly stop the site—they aren't zero-downtime switches.

notes: Current scope: public reads and live contact email. No admin UI, sign-in or message database. SMTP acceptance is not a guarantee of inbox delivery; deployment snapshots are local backups, not off-host disaster recovery.
